text: John William Carson (October 23, 1925 – January 23, 2005) was an American television host, comedian, and writer best known as the host of NBC's The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson (1962–1992). Born in Corning, Iowa, on October 23, 1925, to Ruth Elizabeth Carson (née Hook; 1901–1985) and Homer Lloyd "Kit" Carson (1899–1983), a power company manager, Carson was the second of three children, with an older sister and a younger brother, Richard "Dick" Carson (1929–2021). Growing up in Iowa, he lived in Avoca, Clarinda, and Red Oak before moving to Norfolk, Nebraska, at age 8, where he began developing his talent for entertaining. At age 12, he found a book on magic at a friend's house and purchased a mail-order magician's kit, practicing card tricks on family members and later performing in front of the local Kiwanis Club as "The Great Carsoni" at age 14 for $3 per show. After graduating from high school, he hitchhiked to Hollywood, Los Angeles, where he was arrested and fined $50 for impersonating a midshipman, a story often regarded as apocryphal. Carson joined the United States Navy on June 8, 1943, receiving V-12 Navy College Training Program officer training at Columbia University and Millsaps College. Commissioned an ensign late in the war, he was assigned to the USS Pennsylvania in the Pacific, arriving on August 14, 1945, the same day Imperial Japan announced its surrender. The ship was damaged by a torpedo bomber attack before his arrival and was sent to Guam; after arriving in drydock, Carson, assigned to damage control, supervised the removal of the bodies of 20 servicemen and their effects, describing the experience as "an awful experience" and "a terrible job." He returned to the U.S. and was later assigned to command a troop train for returning servicemen, finishing his service in Guam by decoding encrypted messages. He later recalled that the high point of his military career was performing a magic trick for U.S. Secretary of the Navy James V. Forrestal, who asked if Carson planned to stay in the Navy, prompting Carson to say he wanted to be a magician and perform a card trick, which convinced Forrestal of his ability to entertain. While in the Navy, Carson posted a 15–0–1 amateur boxing record, mostly fought on board the Pennsylvania. After the war, he attended the University of Nebraska, where he joined the Phi Gamma Delta fraternity and continued performing magic (earning $25 per appearance). He majored in journalism initially but switched to speech and drama to become a radio performer, with his college thesis, "How to Write Comedy for Radio," compiling taped skits and jokes from popular radio shows with Carson explaining the comedic technique in a voice-over, allowing him to graduate in three years. He earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in radio and speech with a minor in physics in 1949. Carson began his broadcasting career in 1950 at WOW-AM (now KXSP) and WOW-TV (now WOWT-TV) in Omaha, Nebraska, hosting a morning television program called The Squirrel's Nest, which included interviewing pigeons on the roof of the local courthouse about political corruption. He supplemented his income by serving as master of ceremonies at local church dinners attended by some of the same politicians he had mocked on the radio. The wife of one of these political figures owned stock in a radio station in Los Angeles and in 1951 referred Carson to her brother, who was influential in the emerging television market in Southern California. Carson joined CBS-owned Los Angeles television station KNXT (now KCBS-TV). In 1953, comic Red Skelton, a fan of Carson's low-budget sketch comedy show Carson's Cellar (1951–1953), asked him to join his show as a writer. The following year, Skelton accidentally knocked himself unconscious during rehearsal, an hour before his live show began, and Carson successfully filled in for him. In 1955, Jack Benny invited Carson to appear on one of his programs during the opening and closing segments, where Carson imitated Benny and claimed Benny had copied his gestures; Benny predicted Carson would have a successful career as a comedian. Carson hosted several shows besides Carson's Cellar, including the game show Earn Your Vacation (1954) and the variety show The Johnny Carson Show (1955–1956). He was a guest panelist on the original To Tell the Truth beginning in 1960, becoming a regular panelist from 1961 to 1962. After the primetime Johnny Carson Show failed, Carson moved to New York City to host ABC's Who Do You Trust? (1957–1962), where he met his future sidekick and straight man, Ed McMahon. Although Carson believed moving to daytime television would hurt his career, Who Do You Trust? was a success and became "the hottest item on daytime television" during his six years at ABC, as it was the first show where he could ad lib and interview guests. From his experience as a radio host, Carson later wrote a parody for The New Yorker of former talk show host Dennis Miller having the new role at the time (2000) as an NFL sports announcer, titled "Proverbs of Dennis Miller." NBC's Tonight was the late-night counterpart to its early-morning show Today, originating in 1954 with host Steve Allen, and was somewhat experimental, as the only previous network late-night program was NBC's Broadway Open House (1950–51), which starred Jerry Lester and Dagmar. Tonight was successful; Allen moved to primetime comedy-variety shows in 1957 when Jack Paar became host of Tonight. Paar left the show in 1962. Carson's success on Who Do You Trust? led NBC to invite him to take over Tonight a few months before Paar's departure. Carson declined the offer because he feared the difficulty of interviewing celebrities for 105 minutes each day; Bob Newhart, Jackie Gleason, Groucho Marx, and Joey Bishop also declined. NBC finally convinced Carson to sign by early February 1962. He can be seen discussing his upcoming job for the first time on the February 11, 1962, episode of What's My Line?. Due to Carson having six months left on his ABC contract, NBC used multiple guest hosts until he could take over, including Bishop, Marx, Merv Griffin, Art Linkletter, Arlene Francis, Bob Cummings, Jerry Lewis, Donald O'Connor, and others. Although he continued to have doubts about his new job, Carson became the host of Tonight (later called The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson) on October 1, 1962. After a difficult first year, he overcame his fears. While Tonight under its previous hosts had been successful, especially under Paar, Carson's version eventually did very well in the ratings. Billy Wilder said of Carson: "By the simple law of survival, Carson is the best. He enchants the invalids and the insomniacs as well as the people who have to get up at dawn. He is the Valium and the Nembutal of a nation. No matter what kind of dead-asses are on the show, he has to make them funny and exciting. He has to be their nurse and their surgeon. He has no conceit. He does his work and he comes prepared. If he's talking to an author, he has read the book. Even his rehearsed routines sound improvised. He's the cream of middle-class elegance, yet he's not a mannequin. He has captivated the American bourgeoisie without ever offending the highbrows, and he has never said anything that wasn't liberal or progressive. Every night, in front of millions of people, he has to do the salto mortale [circus parlance for an aerial somersault performed on the tightrope]. What's more, he does it without a net. No rewrites. No retakes. The jokes must work tonight." McMahon followed Carson from Who Do You Trust? as his announcer and sidekick, and Skitch Henderson was installed as the maestro of the NBC Orchestra. McMahon's famous introduction, "Heeeeere's Johnny!!!" was followed by a brief monologue by Carson, often followed by comedy sketches, interviews, and live music. Carson's trademark was a phantom golf swing at the end of his monologues, aimed stage left toward the orchestra (guest hosts sometimes parodied that gesture; Newhart rolled an imaginary bowling ball toward the audience). Paul Anka wrote The Tonight Show's theme song ("Johnny's Theme"), a reworking of his "Toot Sweet"; given lyrics, it was renamed "It's Really Love" and recorded by Annette Funicello in 1959. Before taking over The Tonight Show, Carson wrote lyrics for the song and claimed fifty percent of the song's performance royalties (though the lyrics were never used). The theme is heard being played on sound recordings of Carson's first Tonight Show and was used without interruption through to his last broadcast on May 22, 1992. The Tonight Show was originally produced at NBC's headquarters at 30 Rockefeller Plaza in New York City, with occasional stints in California. The program began videotaping in advance during the Jack Paar days, although during the 1970s NBC fed the live taping from Burbank to New York via satellite for editing. Carson had a talent for quick quips to deal with problems. If the opening monologue fared poorly, the band would start playing "Tea for Two" and Carson danced a softshoe to laughs from the studio audience. Alternatively, Carson might pull the boom microphone close to his face and announce, "Attention K-Mart shoppers, clean up in aisle four!" On May 1, 1972, The Tonight Show moved from 30 Rockefeller Plaza to the NBC Studios in Burbank, California, because of the studio's proximity to celebrities. From 1980, Carson stopped hosting five shows per week; Mondays featured a guest host, leaving Carson to host the other four weeknights. Shows were videotaped in Burbank at 5:30 pm, fed from there to the Central and Eastern Time Zone stations via cross-country television line at 8:30 pm Pacific time (11:30 pm Eastern time), and later sent from Burbank to the Pacific Time Zone stations at 11:30 pm Pacific time. Since only two feeds originated from Burbank, Central Time Zone stations received the Eastern feed one hour earlier at 10:30 pm local time, and Mountain time stations received the Pacific time zone feed one hour later, at 12:30 am local time. Carson announced in April 1979 that he was leaving The Tonight Show after seventeen years hosting the program. At the time, media analysts estimated the show generated 17% of NBC's pre-tax profits. He negotiated a three-year deal to remain with the show in May 1980, reducing the program's length from ninety to sixty minutes while decreasing his workload from four to three nights each week. Tom Snyder's Tomorrow added a half-hour to fill the vacant time. Joan Rivers became the "permanent" guest host from September 1983 until 1986. The Tonight Show then returned to using rotating guest hosts, including comics George Carlin and Garry Shandling. Jay Leno became the exclusive guest host in fall 1987, later joking that although other guest hosts had upped their fees, he had kept his low, assuring himself more bookings. Eventually, Monday night was reserved for Leno and Tuesday night was reserved for The Best of Carson—rebroadcasts usually dating from a year earlier, but occasionally from the 1970s. Although Carson's work schedule became more abbreviated, The Tonight Show remained so successful that his compensation from NBC continued to rise; by the mid-1970s, he had become the highest-paid personality on television, earning about $4 million a year ($19,284,000 today), not including nightclub appearances and his other businesses. Carson refused many offers to appear in films, including title roles in The Thomas Crown Affair and Gene Wilder's role in Blazing Saddles. He also declined director Martin Scorsese's offer to co-star with Robert De Niro in the 1983 film The King of Comedy, with the role of a TV talk-show host then going to Jerry Lewis. In recognition of his 25th anniversary on The Tonight Show, Carson received a personal Peabody Award, the board saying he had "become an American institution, a household word, [and] the most widely quoted American." They also said they "felt the time had come to recognize the contributions that Johnny has made to television, to humor, and to America." In 1973, television personality and self-proclaimed psychic Uri Geller appeared on The Tonight Show. In the NOVA documentary, "James Randi – Secrets of the Psychics," magician and skeptical activist James Randi recalls that Carson "had been a magician himself and was skeptical" of Geller's claimed paranormal powers, and so, prior to the date of taping, Randi was personally asked "to help prevent any trickery." Per Randi's advice, the show's staff prepared its own props without informing Geller and did not let Geller or his staff "anywhere near them." When Geller joined Carson on stage, he appeared surprised that he was not going to be interviewed, but instead was expected to display his abilities using the provided articles. Geller was unable to display any paranormal abilities, saying, "I don't feel strong" and expressing displeasure at feeling like he was being "pressed" to perform by Carson. According to Adam Higginbotham's November 7, 2014, article in The New York Times, the result was a legendary immolation, in which Geller offered up flustered excuses to his host as his abilities failed him again and again. "I sat there for 22 minutes, humiliated," Geller told me, when I spoke to him in September. "I went back to my hotel, devastated. I was about to pack up the next day and go back to Tel Aviv. I thought, That's it — I'm destroyed." However, ironically, this appearance on The Tonight Show, which Carson and Randi had orchestrated to debunk Geller's claimed abilities, backfired. According to Higginbotham, to Geller's astonishment, he was immediately booked on The Merv Griffin Show. He was on his way to becoming a paranormal superstar. "That Johnny Carson show made Uri Geller," Geller said. To an enthusiastically trusting public, his failure only made his gifts seem more real: If he were performing magic tricks, they would surely work every time. Carson played several continuing characters on sketches during the show, including a well-known routine used whenever Carson and a guest toasted each other with glasses of water on the air. Carson would telegraph the joke to the guest: "The king is dead!" Then both would shout "Long live the king!" and take a mouthful of water. Offscreen, Ed McMahon cried, "The king lives!", prompting Carson and the guest to do a spit-take in mock terror. Don Adams, Don Rickles, Mel Brooks, and Dom DeLuise engaged in this routine; one of Adams's Get Smart episodes was even titled "The King Lives?" Although Carson's program moved to Burbank in 1972, NBC's editing and production services for the show remained in New York, requiring that the program be transmitted between the two cities. In 1976, NBC used the Satcom 2 satellite to achieve this, feeding the live taping (which started around 5:30 pm local time) directly to New York, where it would be edited prior to the late-night broadcast. This live feed lasted usually for two to two-and-a-half hours a night. Carson received six Primetime Emmy Awards, the Television Academy's 1980 Governor's Award, and a 1985 Peabody Award. He was inducted into the Television Academy Hall of Fame in 1987. Carson was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1992 and received a Kennedy Center Honor in 1993. Carson remained an American cultural icon even after his retirement in 1992. He adopted a casual, conversational approach with extensive interaction with guests, an approach pioneered by Arthur Godfrey and previous Tonight Show hosts Paar and Steve Allen but enhanced by Carson's lightning-quick wit. A cultural phenomenon, Carson is widely regarded as the King of Late Night Television. Former late-night host and friend David Letterman, as well as many others, have cited Carson's influence.

Carson would signal the joke to the guest by saying, "The king is dead!" followed by both shouting "Long live the king!" and taking a mouthful of water. Offscreen, Ed McMahon would cry, "The king lives!" prompting Carson and the guest to perform a spit-take in mock terror. This routine was performed by Don Adams, Don Rickles, Mel Brooks, and Dom DeLuise; one of Adams's Get Smart episodes was titled "The King Lives?" Although Carson's program moved to Burbank in 1972, NBC's editing and production services remained in New York, requiring the program to be transmitted between the two cities. In 1976, NBC used the Satcom 2 satellite to transmit the live taping, which began around 5:30 pm local time, directly to New York for editing before late-night broadcast. The live feed lasted two to two-and-a-half hours nightly and was uncensored and commercial-free. During commercial breaks, the audio and picture feed continued, capturing risqué language and other content that was later edited out. Satellite ground stations owned by individuals began appearing, and some viewers discovered the live feed, documenting sightings in technical journals. Carson and his staff grew concerned and pressured NBC to stop the satellite transmissions in the early 1980s, after which the satellite link was replaced by microwave transmission until the show's editing facilities moved to Burbank. Carson played himself in the 1964 film Looking for Love and was a surprise guest on the 1970s Bob Hope television special Joys! (a parody of the movie Jaws), which was written and produced by Hal Kanter. Guests on the special included Groucho Marx, George Burns, Telly Savalas, Milton Berle, Red Buttons, Don Adams, Steve Allen, and Harry Ritz. Carson often made jokes at the expense of other celebrities; in 1980, he backed out of a deal to acquire the Aladdin Hotel & Casino in Las Vegas, and a competing group led by Wayne Newton bought the property. According to lawyer Henry Bushkin, Carson became annoyed by media portrayals of him as having "lost" the deal and responded by making jokes about Newton, leading to a feud. Years later, Newton appeared on Larry King Live, stating that "Johnny Carson is a mean-spirited human being" and that Carson had hurt people who would never know, and that Carson turned negative attention toward him. Newton had confronted Carson and ultimately barged into Carson's office at NBC studios, threatening to beat him up unless he stopped making jokes. On February 27, 1982, Carson was arrested for drunk driving on La Cienega Boulevard near Beverly Hills; he was released on his own recognizance. He pleaded no contest to the charges and, in October 1982, received three years probation, a $603 fine, and was required to attend a driver's education alcohol program. His driving privileges were restricted to trips to and from work and alcohol education classes for 90 days. Perry Mason actor Raymond Burr became angry over Carson's jokes about his weight and appeared on The Tonight Show only twice, in 1968 and 1976. On July 2, 1969, Carson launched an on-air attack on The New York Times after a report claimed he earned $75,000 (equivalent to $643,081 in 2024) a week as the highest-paid performer on television. He denied the claim, declined to reveal his pay in a subsequent interview, and called the article "damned unfair." The Times published a follow-up stating its initial reporter "erred" and that $75,000 a week was unlikely. Carson reportedly loathed perceived disloyalty and was furious when former guest hosts John Davidson and Joan Rivers began hosting their own talk shows. Rivers' Fox Network show competed with Carson during the 1986–1987 season before being canceled. On June 24, 2009, following Ed McMahon's death, Rivers spoke highly of McMahon on Larry King Live, saying Carson refused to speak to her again after she got her own show, despite her efforts to apologize. In December 1973, Carson joked about an alleged toilet paper shortage, which viewers believed, leading to panic buying and hoarding across the U.S., causing a real shortage that lasted weeks. Stores and manufacturers had to ration supplies until the panic ended. Carson apologized in January 1974, and the incident became a "classic study" of how rumors spread, with Carson calling references in the article to him "very unfair." Carson successfully sued a portable toilet manufacturer that wanted to call its product "Here's Johnny." He performed a parody of Mister Rogers' Neighborhood, which Rogers noted made him seem "wimpy," and Carson later apologized. In 1979, Carson invested $500,000 (equivalent to $2,166,208 in 2024) in the DeLorean Motor Company. Guest Red Skelton joked on air about the DeLorean and allegations of cocaine trafficking: "That car of yours, the DeLorean? Is that a hopped-up car?" Carson also headed a group of investors who purchased and operated two television stations: KVVU-TV in Henderson, Nevada, acquired in 1979, which was rumored to acquire an NBC affiliation but never did; and KNAT-TV in Albuquerque, New Mexico, purchased in 1982, which faced stiffer competition for programming. Carson sold both stations in 1985 and 1986, with KVVU-TV going to the Meredith Corporation and KNAT to Trinity Broadcasting Network. Carson founded Carson Productions in 1980, which produced The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson from 1980 to 1992 and Late Night with David Letterman from 1982 to 1993, along with Teachers Only (1982–1983), Partners in Crime (1984–1985), Amen (1986–1991), and TV's Bloopers & Practical Jokes (co-produced with Dick Clark Productions, 1984–1993). The company also produced the films The Big Chill (1983) and Desert Bloom (1986). Other business ventures included Johnny Carson Apparel, Inc.—his turtlenecks became a fashion trend—and a failed restaurant franchise. Carson retired from show business on May 22, 1992, at age 66, stepping down as host of The Tonight Show. His farewell was a major media event, emotional for Carson, colleagues, and audiences, and spanned several nights. Several networks went dark for the entire hour of his final show in tribute. After 13 attempts, The Tonight Show won the Emmy for Outstanding Variety, Music or Comedy Series that year, boosted by the penultimate broadcast featuring Robin Williams and Bette Midler as Carson's final two guests. NBC appointed Jay Leno as the new host. Leno and David Letterman soon competed on separate networks. At the end of his final Tonight Show episode, Carson indicated he might return with a new project, but instead chose full retirement, rarely giving interviews and declining to participate in NBC's 75th-anniversary celebrations. He made occasional cameos, including voicing himself on the May 13, 1993, episode of The Simpsons ("Krusty Gets Kancelled"), telephoning David Letterman on a November 1993 episode of Late Show with David Letterman, and appearing in the 1993 NBC special Bob Hope: The First 90 Years. On May 13, 1994, Carson appeared on the Late Show with David Letterman. During a week of shows from Los Angeles, Letterman had Larry "Bud" Melman (Calvert DeForest) deliver "Top Ten Lists" under the guise of a famous personality. On the last show, Letterman said Carson would deliver the list. Instead, DeForest delivered it, insulted the audience, and walked off to polite applause. Letterman then said the card had the wrong list and asked for the real one, prompting the real Carson to emerge behind the curtain as the band played "Johnny's Theme," earning a 90-second standing ovation. Carson then sat behind Letterman's desk as the audience cheered, before departing without speaking, citing acute laryngitis as the reason. This was his last television appearance. Carson played tennis throughout his retirement. He reviewed clips of The Tonight Show in DVD compilations and had humor pieces published in The New Yorker. Prior to his death, Carson occasionally sent jokes to David Letterman, who used them in his monologue, which Carson enjoyed. Letterman later revealed that the monologue in his first broadcast after Carson's death was entirely composed of jokes sent by Carson. Carson's influences included Jack Benny, Red Skelton, Fred Allen, Bob Hope, Groucho Marx, and Jack Paar. His show launched the careers of many performers, especially comedians and musicians. For a comedian, getting Carson to laugh and being invited to the guest chair were considered the highest honors. Notable performers include David Letterman, Freddie Prinze, Robin Williams, Jay Leno, Jerry Seinfeld, Arsenio Hall, Jeff Foxworthy, Ellen DeGeneres, Rodney Dangerfield, Joan Rivers, David Brenner, Tim Allen, Drew Carey, Howie Mandel, Roseanne Barr, and Don Rickles. Carson succeeded The Ed Sullivan Show as a showcase for talent and continued a vaudeville-style variety show. In 1966, Carson popularized Milton Bradley's game Twister when he played it with actress Eva Gabor, causing a surge in popularity. Comedians who credited Carson as an influence include David Letterman, Jay Leno, Conan O'Brien, Dennis Miller, Bill Maher, Joan Rivers, Larry Wilmore, Ray Romano, Don Rickles, Bob Newhart, Angie Dickinson, Carl Reiner, Mel Brooks, Dick Cavett, Norm Macdonald, David Steinberg, Jerry Seinfeld, Ellen DeGeneres, Garry Shandling, Steve Martin, Ray Combs, Arsenio Hall, Craig Ferguson, Orson Bean, and Jimmy Fallon. Brian Wilson wrote a song titled "Johnny Carson" in 1977 as a tribute, released on the Beach Boys Love You album. In 1983, he was awarded American Library Association Honorary Membership. Despite his on-camera demeanor, Carson was introverted off-camera and avoided most parties, being called "the most private public man who ever lived." Dick Cavett recalled that Carson struggled socially, saying, "I've hardly ever met anybody who had as hard a time as he did." George Axelrod said, "Socially, he doesn't exist. The reason is that there are no television cameras in living rooms. If human beings had little red lights in the middle of their foreheads, Carson would be the greatest conversationalist on Earth." Musician John Oates noted that Carson was subdued until the camera lights came on, when he became "Johnny Carson" with his pencil-tapping habit, and then stopped when the commercial began. He normally refused to discuss politics, social controversies, his childhood, or private life, offering pre-written answers such as "Yes, I did," "Not a bit of truth in that rumor," and "No, kumquats." Carson opposed the Vietnam War and capital punishment, favored racial equality, and was against criminalizing extramarital sex and pornography. He avoided explicitly mentioning his views on The Tonight Show, saying he "hates to be pinned down" because it would "hurt me as an entertainer," and in 1970 explained that in his living room he would support liberalization of abortion and divorce laws, but did not want to express political views on air because he "would love to have taken on Billy Graham" but had "nothing to gain and everything to lose." He seldom invited political figures because he "didn't want it to become a political forum" and did not want the show used to influence viewers. In his book, Carson's former lawyer Henry Bushkin stated he was "by instinct and upbringing definitely Republican, but of an Eisenhower sort that we don't see much of anymore—overall, anti-big: anti-big government, anti-big money, anti-big bullies, anti-big blowhards." Carson served as MC for Ronald Reagan's inaugural gala in 1981 at Frank Sinatra's request. In October 1982, Carson pleaded no contest to a misdemeanor charge of driving with a blood alcohol level above the legal limit, while charges of driving under the influence and driving without a license were dropped. This stemmed from an arrest in February 1982, when he was pulled over shortly after leaving an Italian restaurant with his wife. He was fined $603, placed on three years probation, ordered to attend a driver's education alcohol program, and had his license restricted for 90 days to trips to and from work and classes. His lawyer Robert Shapiro advised a trial, but Carson wanted to avoid media attention and chose to plead no contest, saying in a monologue, "I regret the incident, and you will never see me do that again." As an adult, Carson was not a regular churchgoer, though he was raised as a Methodist and attended Christian Endeavor meetings in high school. In October 1949, Carson married Jody Wolcott in North Platte, Nebraska. The marriage was volatile with infidelities by both parties and ended in divorce in May 1963. Carson married Joanne Copeland on August 17 of the same year. After a protracted divorce in 1972, Copeland received a settlement of nearly US$500,000 (equivalent to $3,758,552 in 2024), plus an annual hundred thousand in alimony, and "a pretty nice little art collection." She later married again and died in California at age 83 in 2015, with no children. In October 1949, Carson married Jody Wolcott in North Platte, Nebraska; their marriage was volatile, marked by infidelities from both parties, and ended in divorce in May 1963. That same year, on August 17, he married Joanne Copeland. After a lengthy divorce in 1972, Copeland received a settlement of nearly US$500,000 (equivalent to $3,758,552 in 2024), plus an annual alimony of $100,000, and also received "a pretty nice little art collection." She later married again, divorced, and died in California at age 83 in 2015, having no children. In fall 1971, while going through divorce proceedings with Copeland, Carson met 40-year-old former model Joanna Holland (née Ulrich, 1931–2025) at the 21 Club in New York City, where she had previously worked with fashion designer Mollie Parnis. Carson arranged for her to take his phone call through Parnis several days later. Holland, also a divorcée with a son, Tim, from a prior marriage, became Carson’s partner; their first date in late October 1971—dinner and a show—was also Carson’s 46th birthday celebration, and for the next year he reportedly called her every day at 4:30 p.m. In May 1972, Carson's Tonight Show moved production to Burbank, and soon after, Holland and her 11-year-old son joined him in California, where he purchased a US$500,000 Bel-Air mansion originally owned by filmmaker Mervyn LeRoy. At the Tonight Show's 10th-anniversary party on September 30, 1972, at the Beverly Hills Hotel, Carson announced they had been secretly married that afternoon in Santa Monica, shocking his associates. Holland, who had previously traveled to luxury destinations like Biarritz, Monte Carlo, and Saint Moritz with her ex-husband, introduced Carson to Western European travel, including visits to Hôtel du Cap in Antibes and Wimbledon Championships, which he enjoyed due to being unknown there and avoiding fans. The couple separated in November 1982, reportedly due to Carson’s infidelity, with Carson moving to their Malibu beach house; on March 8, 1983, Holland filed for divorce. The case concluded in August 1985 with an 80-page settlement, in which she received US$20 million (equivalent to $58,471,535 in 2024) in combined assets—including the Bel-Air mansion, three Manhattan apartments (at the Pierre, on Fifth Avenue, and on 62nd Street), a Rolls-Royce, a Mercedes-Benz, and an economy car—and monthly alimony of US$35,000 for 64 months. Carson later used the financial details of the divorce as comedic material on The Tonight Show. Holland’s son, Tim Holland (later known as Joe), died in May 1994 from pulmonary embolism. Joanna Holland died in July 2025 at age 93. On June 20, 1987, Carson married Alexis Maas, and the marriage lasted until his death in 2005. Carson reportedly joked, "My giving advice on marriage is like the captain of the Titanic giving lessons on navigation." He had three sons with his first wife: Christopher (1950–2025), Kim Arthur "Ricky" (1951–1991), and Barry William "Cory" (born 1953). His middle son, Ricky, died in a car accident in 1991 while shooting nature photographs; upon Carson’s return to air, he delivered a lengthy tribute to Ricky, which was interrupted by producer Fred de Cordova, who signaled for the segment to end, leading to de Cordova being banned from the studio floor. During his final Tonight Show broadcasts in May 1992, Carson brought his two surviving sons onto stage, and the final episode included one of Ricky’s nature photographs in the credit roll. In 1981, Carson founded the John W. Carson Foundation to support children, education, and health services. In August 2010, the foundation reported receiving $156 million (equivalent to $251,157,608 in 2024) from a personal trust established years before his death, making it the largest Hollywood charity; as of 2022, it continues to support charitable causes. In November 2004, Carson donated $5.3 million to the University of Nebraska Foundation to support the Hixson–Lied College of Fine and Performing Arts Department of Theater Arts, creating the Johnny Carson School of Theater and Film. After his death, the estate donated another $5 million to the university, and on November 4, 2011, a $1 million donation was announced to create the Johnny Carson Opportunity Scholarship Fund. On October 22, 2021, the foundation made an additional $5 million donation to augment the scholarship fund. Carson also donated to causes in his adopted hometown of Norfolk, including the Carson Cancer Center at Faith Regional Health Services, the Elkhorn Valley Museum, and the Johnny Carson Theater at Norfolk Senior High School, and to the Northeast Community College Lifelong Learning Center in honor of his favorite teacher, Miss Fay Gordon, who had appeared on his show multiple times; he fulfilled a promise to attend her 100th-birthday party. Carson, an amateur astronomer, was a close friend of Carl Sagan, who frequently appeared on The Tonight Show; Sagan’s distinctive way of saying words like "billions" of stars led Carson to mock him with "BILL-ions and BILL-ions." Carson was the first to contact Sagan’s wife, Ann Druyan, with condolences after Sagan’s death in 1996. He owned several telescopes, including a top-of-the-line unit. In 1981, the minor planet 1981 EM4 (3252 Johnny) was named in his honor, and a star was also nicknamed after him that year. Carson was an amateur drummer and appeared on a 1979 60 Minutes segment practicing at home on a drum set given to him by jazz musician Buddy Rich, who had the most appearances on The Tonight Show. Gore Vidal, a frequent guest and friend, wrote about Carson’s personality in his 2006 memoir. Carson was an avid tennis player; when he sold a Malibu house to John McEnroe and Tatum O'Neal, McEnroe was required to give Carson six tennis lessons. Carson’s primary tennis teacher was Bob Trapenberg, who taught him and traveled with him to Wimbledon. Carson was also a private pilot; his flight logbook and jacket were donated after his death to the Experimental Aircraft Association in Oshkosh, Wisconsin. On March 19, 1999, Carson suffered a severe heart attack at his Malibu home and was hospitalized in Santa Monica, where he underwent quadruple-bypass surgery. Carson had been a heavy smoker for decades, often smoking on-camera, at one point consuming four packs of Pall Mall cigarettes a day; he reportedly said, "These things are killing me" as early as the mid-1970s, and his younger brother recalled that during their last conversation, Carson repeatedly said, "Those damn cigarettes." In 2002, he declined an offer to appear at NBC’s 75th anniversary. In September 2002, Carson revealed he had emphysema but denied being terminally ill. On January 23, 2005, Carson died at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles from respiratory failure due to emphysema. His body was cremated, and the ashes were given to his wife, Alexis Maas. No public memorial service was held; he was also survived by his younger brother, Dick, an Emmy Award–winning director of shows such as the Merv Griffin Show and Wheel of Fortune. Numerous tributes were paid to Carson after his death, including a statement by then-President George W. Bush, all recognizing the deep affection for him. On January 31, Late Show with David Letterman paid tribute with former executive producer Peter Lassally and bandleader Doc Severinsen; Letterman said that for 30 years, people wanted to end their days being "tucked in by Johnny," and the monologue he performed consisted entirely of jokes sent to him by Carson in his final months. Doc Severinsen ended the show by performing and playing one of Carson’s two favorite songs, "Here's That Rainy Day," with Tommy Newsom and Ed Shaughnessy. The Tonight Show with Jay Leno also honored Carson with guests Ed McMahon, Bob Newhart, Don Rickles, Drew Carey, and k.d. lang. On his final appearance, Carson stated that he and Ed McMahon were good friends who shared drinks and dinners, with a camaraderie spanning 46 years. The 2005 film The Aristocrats was dedicated to Carson. The Simpsons’ seventh episode of season 16, "Mommie Beerest," was dedicated to his memory. At the first Comedy Awards on Comedy Central, the Johnny Carson Award was given to David Letterman; at the second Annual Comedy Awards, it was given to Don Rickles. A two-hour documentary, Johnny Carson: King of Late Night, aired on PBS on May 14, 2012, as part of the American Masters series, narrated by Kevin Spacey and featuring interviews with family, fellow comedians, and protégés. A park is named in his memory in Burbank, across from the former NBC Studios.
